narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. While accepted students typically rank around the middle of their class (average decile near 6), you placed in the bottom decile. This low ranking signaled to the model a pattern strongly associated with later bar exam difficulty.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure. At 26, it sits well below the average of 37 seen among students who were accepted, indicating weaker preparation in the skills the bar exam tests.

Your undergraduate GPA was the only factor that worked in your favor, slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure. However, at 2.8 compared to an average of 3.23 among accepted students, its positive effect was not nearly enough to offset the other signals.

Taken together, these academic performance indicators created a clear picture for the model that the odds of passing the bar on the first try were low. To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic performance, consider retaking the LSAT to achieve a significantly higher score, and then reapply. Strengthening these core predictors will be the most direct way to change future model outcomes. (248 words)
